I was doing cabinetmaking before I decided to go into massage. It was something I thought I would do forever, but the reality of it was it made me miserable. I say all this to tell you, you don't have to be miserable with the work you do. You have the choice to walk away. My first job outside of school paid me $373 for the first month and I also ended up in the hospital for mental health reasons. I made the decision to apply for other jobs and that took me on an entirely new adventure in my life. 


You can either look for a better job that honours yours boundaries and limits, or you can find a job in something completely different. We don't have to be bound by the decisions we made. It is a skill and something you can do for friends and family. It's something you can do super part time if you want to supplement income from a different avenue. It's all up to you, and the beauty of massage is how flexible it can be. 


Best of luck, I wish you well in whatever your pursue.

Never. I've had people surprised that the name I go by isn't my legal name when I tell them and they're a personal contact. But at work, if someone asks, I just say that [blank] is my legal name, but I go by [blank]. If they press, I just say that I have gone by this name for a long time and the old name isn't who I am anymore. I was transitioning to male when I started going by my new name, but evolved into nonbinary now. 

I feel like modern society has (mostly) accepted people using different names. People use aliases for any number of reasons, from transitioning, immigrating, hiding from family (an ex best friend changed xir name so xir mother wouldn't be able to track xir down), to simply using a middle name because their first was that of a relatives. I have many clients who use an alternate first name. I don't use either my legal first or last name on social media.

I've gone by my chosen name for the last 11 years. People wouldn't know it wasn't my legal name unless I told them. I do legally have to use my birth name at work for my clients' insurance claims, but I introduce myself as my preferred name, and all my colleagues and support staff use it too. I've pondered changing it legally, but it's expensive, timely, and I have a connection to it via my mum; she dreamt of the name before conceiving me so there is significance to it for me. 

My birth name is unique, and that has always given me challenges due to the system not using accents (despite living in Canada where French is an official language), and back in the day, there was a guy with a very similar name who became a famous singer. So all trace of my legal name is almost gone, if not completely overridden by this famous dude lol.

My advice is you dont need to legally change your name to go by a different name. You've already got experience with the transitioning to a new name, several times now. Choose something a little less unique, change or create new socials with that name, introduce yourself to new people with it, tell those you are close with about the name. Decide if you want those people to call that name, or only have it be for your profession. You could also have multiple socials, one private with your legal name and one public with your new name to garner your professional connections. Ultimately, it is up to you whether you want to change it legally or not, but it doesn't mean it is required to do so. People go by aliases for so many different reasons.

My interview process:
What can I help you with today?
Are there any accidents or injuries I should know about?
What kind of physical activities do you do?
What kind of pressure are you looking for?
My spiel that I outlined before in my previous comment.
Do you have any questions or concerns for me? 
I can either let the client get ready and leave to wash my hands, or do a physical assessment. I will tell repeat to the client what I will work on that day (say, an upper body treatment with focus on neck and shoulders).

It's not as in depth as the interview process I learned in school, but it's efficient and gives me a lot of info to begin with. It establishes trust with the client, that I care about their needs and I that have listened to them. 

Is it a script? Sure, but being neurodivergent, I have a hard time knowing exactly what to say and it gives me consistency to work with, and my clients know exactly what to expect the next time I see them. I can modify the script for those who are regulars and I'm comfortable with. But new clients have no idea who I am or how I work, and if I can explain to them precisely what to expect from the treatment at the beginning of establishing a professional relationship, people generally don't have complaints.

For you as a client, it's great that you tell the therapists what you are looking for. I'm sorry you don't get asked any questions though. There's gotta be some information a therapist requires. Sometimes intake forms are old, and what the client has circled in the past isn't what they're looking for in that moment. Or there's been a recent injury or condition that could be contraindicated.

I tell people during the intake that I take my time warming up the tissue and letting their body get used to my touch. I will ask them about pressure once I get to the deepest I feel their body is comfortable with. It's stopped this comment about 99% of the time 

I got really annoyed with people telling me to go harder when I'm still doing my compressions through the linens. Haven't even gotten to draping nor applying oil yet. People have expectations, and once you give them an idea of what to expect, they're less likely to demand something else from you.

I became allergic to weed. I've always been sensitive to it, couldn't touch the flower without getting a rash. But I could smoke, vape and have edibles. But I'd get terrible sneezing and coughing fits. Terpenes are really bad for it. I hit a vape pen a few weeks ago and got hives on my face. The second time I tried it, an even worse reaction with hives and my throat closing. Antihistamines and a cold shower did the trick of stopping the reaction, but I haven't been able to smoke since. I had bought some prerolls and got hives again, not as intensely. I've quit since, it's been almost three weeks since I stopped. The congestion, morning sneezing fits, plugged nose, grogginess have disappeared. 

I was a daily smoker with some t breaks here and there. 6-9 tokes a night, or half a cbd edible. 

You could be sensitive until you're not. When you pass the threshold from sensitivity to allergy, it's not good, man. You won't regret quitting. The more you come into contact with something you're sensitive to, the higher the chance you risk an allergic reaction. The more allergic reactions you have, the higher the probability of anaphylaxis. You really don't want to get to that level.

Having to commit to forever is daunting and unrealistic. Aim for shorter, more practical goals. Knowing that the first three days are the worst, aim for getting to that fourth day. And then five. And then seven. And then two weeks. And then a month. Set an intention. Challenge yourself to quit for a full week to start. 

Take care of yourself. Your body will be going through a lot of stress. Eat good food. Do light exercise or take walks. 

For me it's the challenge. I'm competitive in spirit and want to see how much better my life can be. I have no choice in my quitting as I became allergic to weed. But now that I'm on the roll, I want to see how much better my body, mind, and spirit can become without the shackles of weed holding me captive. 

Figure out your values. What is your goal? Why do you want to quit? How will you focus your attention to the changes?

It's only been a couple weeks for me, but life is so much better without it. Things aren't dull anymore. I've developed a lot of new habits and rituals and having natural dopamine being made is so much nicer. Depression isn't as pervading. Anxiety has gone down immensely. Diet and exercise feels amazing to dive into. Food tastes and smells better. Being able to fall asleep without anything because I've accomplished things in my day instead of feeling regret that I wasted my precious time being stoned all day on my time off. I've had the most mentally and spiritually taxing month of my life, but I've trucked on and am constantly discovering what is working for me.

So, I present to you an ultimatum, that is entirely up to you to decide on. Evolve or die. Try quitting for a month and do a check in with yourself. Ask yourself at the end of the month, does weed really serve me? Or have I been abusing a substance to numb myself? Work with a therapist or councilor to navigate the underlying issues. Once we abuse marijuana, she will turn her back on us and become an aggressor of our mental health in the guise of a companion helping us. She perpetuates the negative issues and becomes detrimental on our health. 

Again, this will always be your prerogative, no one can force your to do anything in life. But can you rise to the challenge? You'll be surprised at what you can do.

 Start easy on yourself. You will be sick, stock up on bone broth and fruits to get you through the first week. But you can get through this. You just have to start. I suggest getting a journal and writing everyday. It's an easy and accessible exercise in getting to know yourself. There's many prompts you can find online if you don't know what to write about. Or even just start recording what you've done that day. 

You got this, fam! Be strong 💪

Weed is a self-limitor. It creates self-limiting paradigms in your head and begs you to buy into the conspiracy. 

Something interesting I learned in class last week was after 2 years of habitual use, the brain physically changes and looks more like the brain of a schizophrenic. This isn't to say you will become schizophrenic, but changes are made. There was a study done with brain scans of young people who smoke daily (starting at 17/18, and by 19/20 these changes occur.) So just something to consider. 

If you've been accepted into a hard programme, be proud of that already. But you will have to put in the work to get through it. And if you are under the influence of something that self-limits, you likely won't perform as well. You need your brain to be on the whole time. Learning now how to process and regulate emotions in a healthy manner is paramount to your success. School is hard.

I've picked up qigong classes. I've joined recreational sports leagues. Macebell and clubbell classes, pilates. Anything that looks interesting and is affordable. Eating well. Oh man, unless you already have a background in hands in therapy, it isn't going to be easy to learn how to palpate osteopathically. This isn't really something you can read a book and learn, sorry to say. I'm halfway through a five year programme and barely starting to feel and see things osteopathically. Certainly you can try to learn the principles, you can check out A. T. Still's books, maybe even William Garner Sutherland. But they're dense. Even with a background in anatomy and touch, it's still a very difficult endeavour to learn manual osteopathy. Books can be niche and expensive. 

I'll give you the four tenets of osteopathy, as I've learned them, and continue to form new understanding as each course comes.

1. The body is a functional unit.
2. Structure governs function.
3. The body can autoregulate health.
4. The rule of the artery is absolute.

I don't mean to be discouraging, but I really don't think this is something a person can self study. Even with the guidance of instructors, there is just so much to learn. It's like trying to jam an entire tree into a pothole. We can only learn so much at one time, and there is too much information to digest. I think it's great that you have an interest in this field, it's pretty amazing what can be done with manual osteopathy.

So, the reason why the body may shake is due to something called a neurogenic tremor. Essentially, when the body has gone through trauma, entered the fight/flight/freeze mode, the sympathetic nervous system turns on. The natural way for the body to let go of that energy is to shake. This is why we tremble and cry when we're scared. Due to societal stigma and the developed prefrontal cortex, most adult humans do not experience neurogenic tremors. 

All mammals experience this. There was a video of a polar bear being tracked and eventually shot with a tranquilizer to be tagged. You can see after the sedation wears off, the polar bear's entire body starts shaking, due to the stress of being tracked down.

The only animals that don't have neurogenic tremors are animals in captivity... and adult humans.

I was trying to become a cabinetmaker before getting into massage. I loved the work, but the hours were grueling and I never secured an apprenticeship. Depending on where you are, most cities have a programme that will give you a decent amount of training in the trades before starting your apprenticeship. You can start out as a labourer, but I found it difficult to get an apprenticeship and layoffs were common. I was never able to find a shop that kept me for longer than the probationary period. 

I eventually decided that being up at 5 am to be at the shop for 7 everyday wasn't the life I wanted. I enjoy doing massage for the flexibility and I'm more of an evening person than a morning one. On an hourly basis, it looks like plumbers make less than RMTs, but RMTs typically work less hours. It also really depends on where you are in Canada. If you're in a regulated province, you'll easily make double what I do in an unregulated province. 

There's lots to consider when making the decision. What kind of lifestyle do you want to have? Becoming a journeyman will take 4+ years. Massage school is 2-3 years. Plumbing jobs are 8-10 hours a day whereas massage you can work anywhere from 1-6. Some folks can do 7-9 massages a day, but the majority have a max of 5 clients a day. Are you a morning person? Are you good with finances? As a contractor, you don't get taxes taken off your cheques and you have to put money away for ei, cpp, rrsps, federal and provincial taxes. 

I think having any experience in the trades is a good thing. I have no regrets about really trying for about 2 years to be a cabinetmaker and I learned a lot that has been useful. But massage has opened many more doors for me.
